input.question: If the Hubble telescope can zoom into the far reaches of the galaxy, why can't we just point it at Earth-like planets to see if they have water/vegetation etc.
input.ground_truth: We can't "see" earth like planets. They are too far away. The hubble telescope is great for seeing faint and far away things. We can see faint stars. We can see distant galaxies. We can see BOTH of these things because they give off light. We point our telescope at these and basically "leave the shutter open". This gathers light over an extended period of time. **Planets do not give off light. They only reflect light. This is not enough light to actually "see" the planet itself.** And on the remote chance we do see it, it isn't in enough detail to see the surface. The reason we know planets exist is not because we "see" them. It is because we see the effect they have on the stars they orbit.

Okay, let’s imagine the Hubble telescope is like a really big pair of binoculars that can look very, very far away. But even though it’s super powerful, looking at things that are super far away is like trying to see a tiny ant on the other side of a football field with your eyes closed. 

Now, if we want to look at a planet that’s like Earth but very, very far away, it’s like trying to see a tiny marble in a giant playground from your house. The planet is so small and so far away that even Hubble’s big eyes can’t see if it has grass or water. It’s just too tiny and too far for Hubble to show us all those details.

We need even bigger and better telescopes, or special ways to look (like using clever tricks with light), to see those tiny details on faraway planets. Right now, Hubble is really good at looking far, but not so good at seeing tiny things up close that are far away.
